hook.text: Freeze a model's code, and it still gets worse. Nothing in the repository moved. The world it learned from did: new customers, new tactics, a sensor swapped for one that reports in other units.

plan.text: This round is everything after training: versioning, testing, shipping, and watching a model in production. Twelve questions are worked through here, and five go quickly.

q1.text: Question one. What is MLOps, and how does it differ from traditional DevOps? It brings DevOps practices to machine learning: automation, monitoring, and continuous integration and delivery, or CI CD. But it adds a moving part: data.
q1.spoken: Question one. What is em-el-ops, and how does it differ from traditional DevOps? It brings DevOps practices to machine learning: automation, monitoring, and continuous integration and delivery, or CI CD. But it adds a moving part: data.

q1-three.text: A traditional app is code plus config. An ML system is code, plus data, plus the trained model they produce, and all three must be versioned, tested and reproducible. And because a model decays while its code stays frozen, monitoring and retraining are part of the job from day one.

q2.text: Questions two and three. What do you need to version to reproduce a model? And how do you version training data?

q2-four.text: Four things: the code, in git; the data, as a snapshot; the config, meaning hyperparameters, feature definitions and random seeds; and the trained artifact. A container image pins the libraries underneath.

q2-data.text: Data is the awkward one. Track snapshots beside each commit with a tool like DVC, data version control; query a warehouse with time travel, as of a past date; or write to immutable, date-stamped paths. The goal is the exact training set behind any past model.

q2-seed.text: Why log the seed? Train a random forest on handwritten digits twenty times, changing nothing but the seed, and held-out accuracy runs from ninety-six point one to ninety-seven point eight percent. Fix the seed, and every prediction matches, run after run.

q2-why.text: So a one-point gain may just be a lucky seed: judge a change over several seeds, not one. And reproducible means the same code, data and config give back the same artifact.

q4.text: Questions four and five. How do you design a CI CD pipeline for ML? And what is an evaluation gate, and why is it essential? The pipeline validates the new data, tests the feature transforms, trains on a versioned dataset, gates the result, promotes it in the registry, and rolls it out in stages: shadow, canary, full.

q4-gate.text: Code, data or a schedule can trigger it, so new models arrive with nobody looking. The gate looks for you: the candidate must beat the production model on a fixed holdout set, or the build fails. Without it, a retrain can quietly ship a regression.

q4-slice.text: The follow-up is what beat means. Simulate a retrain on last month's data, which held almost none of one customer group. The candidate wins overall, seventy-seven percent to seventy-five. On that group, one customer in twenty, it falls from seventy-nine percent to forty-six, worse than a coin flip.

q4-floor.text: So the gate also sets a floor on every slice that matters, not just the total.

q6.text: Question six. How do you monitor a model in production? In two layers. Operational health: latency at the median and the tail, error rate, throughput and resources.

q6-model.text: Model health: the input feature distributions, the distribution of predictions, and once labels arrive, live accuracy, precision and recall.

q6-wire.text: Log inputs and predictions, so you can debug and replay, and wire every alert to an action: retrain, or roll back.

q6-first.text: Labels can take weeks, so the inputs and the predictions are what you'll see move first. That's where drift comes in.

q7.text: Questions seven and eight. Data drift versus concept drift versus performance degradation? And how do you detect and respond to concept drift?

q7-defs.text: Data drift is the inputs shifting: a new kind of customer, a sensor's new units. Concept drift is the link from input to label shifting: fraud tactics evolve, so the same features mean something new. Degradation is the drop in quality either can cause.

q7-data.text: Simulate a model trained on two features. Next quarter, the first one shifts. Its drift score, the population stability index or PSI, reads point nine one: a loud alarm.

q7-rises.text: Yet accuracy rises, from eighty percent to eighty-four. This time, the rule the model learned still held where the inputs moved.

q7-concept.text: Another quarter, and no input moves at all. Every PSI, on both features and on the predictions, stays under point oh two. But the relationship changed, and accuracy falls to sixty-one.

q7-respond.text: The inputs rang for the harmless shift and stayed silent for the harmful one. Confirming concept drift takes labels: as they arrive, track accuracy and calibration over time, against stable cohorts where you can. Then respond in proportion: an alert, a retrain on recent data, or new features if the change is structural.

q9.text: Questions nine and ten. What is the population stability index? And how do you detect drift when labels are delayed or unavailable?

q9-how.text: PSI compares one feature's distribution now with its distribution in training. Cut the training values into ten buckets of equal share, then add up, over the buckets, the difference in share times the log of their ratio.

q9-example.text: In a simulation, a slight shift scores point oh one, and a large one, one point four. Under point one is called stable, and over point two needs action, but those are conventions, not significance tests.

q9-labels.text: With labels late, PSI or a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on each input, and on the predictions, is your early warning. It can show that something moved; it can't prove the model got worse. For that, measure outcomes: delayed labels, audits, or a small randomized slice.

q9-noise.text: Calibrate the threshold to your traffic, because PSI is noisy on small samples. With no drift at all, a window of a hundred values scores over point one almost half the time. A window of a thousand: never, in two thousand tries.

q9-edges.text: And leave the outer buckets open. Edges cut at the training minimum and maximum drop anything beyond them from the count. Simulate a fifth of values arriving past anything seen in training: closed edges read point oh three, stable. Open ones read point two five.

q11.text: Question eleven. How do you roll out a new model version safely? In stages, with a way back from each.

q11-shadow.text: First, shadow: mirror live traffic to the new model, log its predictions, and return none of them. You compare outputs, latency and errors under real load, with no user exposed.

q11-canary.text: Then a canary: send one to five percent of traffic to the new version, and watch the business and model guardrails. Ramp up while they hold, and send traffic straight back the moment they don't.

q11-rollback.text: That's the rollback, and it should be a config change, not a redeploy: the previous artifact and its serving config stay in the registry, and the traffic weights flip back. The catch is state. Feature store writes, A B assignment logs and caches the new model touched don't flip back with it, so rehearse it.

q12.text: Question twelve. What is A B testing for models, and how does it differ from shadow testing? A shadow test can check parity, in outputs and latency, but never impact, because users only see the current model's predictions. Nobody can click a recommendation they were never shown.

q12-ab.text: An A B test serves each variant to real users and compares business metrics, like click-through or conversion. It measures impact, at the price of exposure.

q12-champ.text: Champion and challenger names the routine: the champion serves production, challengers run beside it, in shadow or on a canary slice, and one takes over only by beating it on live traffic, not just on an offline benchmark.

r-registry.text: A model registry versions trained artifacts with their metadata: the data version, hyperparameters, evaluation metrics and deployment history. It enforces promotion from staging to production, and turns a rollback into a lookup rather than a rebuild.

r-retrain.text: Retraining has four triggers: a schedule, a drift alert, live accuracy or a proxy falling below a threshold, and enough new labeled data. Continuous training automates them, and every version it produces goes through the same gate and staged rollout.

r-bluegreen.text: Blue-green keeps two full environments. Blue serves while green gets the new model and warms up; traffic flips in one switch, and flips back if anything breaks. Near-zero downtime and instant rollback, for the cost of running both. A canary is the gradual version.

r-tracking.text: Experiment tracking, with tools like MLflow or Weights and Biases, logs every run's hyperparameters, metrics, code version and artifacts. Without it, nobody can say which run made the model in production.
r-tracking.spoken: Experiment tracking, with tools like em-el-flow or Weights and Biases, logs every run's hyperparameters, metrics, code version and artifacts. Without it, nobody can say which run made the model in production.

r-package.text: And to package a model, serialize the artifact, pin the runtime and dependencies, and build a container so serving matches training. Exporting to ONNX, a framework-neutral format, frees it from the training library and opens faster runtimes.
r-package.spoken: And to package a model, serialize the artifact, pin the runtime and dependencies, and build a container so serving matches training. Exporting to onyx, a framework-neutral format, frees it from the training library and opens faster runtimes.

close.text: Versioned, gated, watched and reversible: that's a model you can leave running.
